---
title: "A Memorial Service"
author: "DK"
date: "2025-10-12"
categories: [remembrance]
---

A difficult set of questions arose before the event.

Due to a sudden traffic accident, we found ourselves preparing a service of remembrance.

[Just two months earlier, during our visit to Korea, she shared with us her future plans to re-visit her home country and her love for painting.]

Those attending would be primarily ethnic Koreans—mostly first-generation immigrants and their children.

Many of the older attendees would preferr a Korean-language service, while the younger generation, less fluent in Korean, would be unable to follow. After thoughtful discussion, it was decided that the service would be conducted in English, so the younger family members could participate more fully.

The greater challenge was in determining the nature of the service—how it should be framed, and which customs or traditions to follow. Should it take on a religious form or remain secular?

For those that live in Utah, such matters seldom arose and discussed openly. Lack of contact from ecclesiastical representatives suggested her recent absence from the congregational activity.

This left her husband and three sons with the responsibility of planning the service. I was invited to officiate, at a ceremony to be held 1,400 miles away in a lakeside city.

As we boarded the plane, we received the finalized program. It followed the tradition of **The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (**예수 그리스도 후기 성도 교회), the faith community she and her family had attended during the years we knew them.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Between the time we learned of her passing and the funeral was 17 days. We received the plan in bits and pieces. Because of the distance and lack of involvement, I began to question or second guess some of the decisions – I murmured.

However, when I met the family and saw the arrangement, on the morning of the service, my heart was cleansed and I was embarrassed of the attitude I had taken.

The family tried their utmost to honor, remember and love their wife, mother, and a grandmother.

In the absence of one over-riding preference or tradition, the family had adopted an universal approach to saying goodbye to a mortal existence.

They remembered her fierce determination, tenacity and hard work. Her appreciation for education and knowledge.

She studied painting, late in her life. She enjoyed painting family portraits. She was working on a painting of her third son, the night of her passing.

They honored her by recalling her teachings and wisdom.

She had a remarkable intellect. Had she been born in this modern era, she would have been a medical doctor.

As they recounted her life, thought of my own shortcomings and limitations. As I normally do, I pledged to be a better person, husband and father.

They expressed hope and assurance in reuniting in the life or phase hereafter.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

As the autumn mid-day cast its intermittent sunshine amidst cloud cover, she was interred in a site chosen by the family. As a final resting place until her resurrection or uniting of her body and spirit.

As services ended and family members said their goodbyes, recalled words spoken by her during the Holladay period.

This was when I was dating Sister K.

> Don't see her as she now is, working in a menial, physical job to support her education. She is from a good family.

She was saying in essence,

> But rather see her as she was and is to become

Enforcing a Christian belief that we had a noble beginning and that we are here to prove ourselves to be worthy of our eternal life.

That we all

> ...are taken home to that God who gave them life. 
(Alma 40:11)

Thank you 황이모 for your life and examples.
